parts.label: Part 4
parts.article:
Good morning. My name is Caroline Stewart and I’d like to give you an overview of the research we’ve been carrying out to learn more about the elephants living in the Amboseli National Park in Kenya.

Let me start by telling you a little about the methodology we use. We’ve been studying this population of elephants for nearly 40 years and we’ve collected a wealth of information about individual elephants. We now have a database of 2,500 elephants from the area and we know the month and year of their birth as well as who was the mother of each one. More recently, one of my colleagues has been examining the pattern of elephant relationships within and between the families in more detail. He’s done this by using audio equipment to record and then playback the calls that are made by the elephants. And in addition to that, for some time we’ve been using DNA analysis to investigate these relationships. The findings were significant. For example, for a long time we’d suspected that elephants live in a very complex social system and one thing we found from our research is that this social system is made up of a large number of different layers, not just parent and child, but also brother and sister and so on.

Another important discovery was that elephants can be very cooperative as much as chimps, in fact. We conducted an experiment in which two of the elephants brought food within reach by pulling simultaneously on the ends of a rope. It was a surprise even to us that they managed to do it. Another finding was just how flexible elephants can be. They may live in smaller or larger groups depending on environmental conditions. So for example, an adult female and her calves might leave their larger groups for days or weeks. A good example of this was two years ago when there was not enough rain. Many left the herd and moved to new areas in order to survive. We also discovered that elephants can show emotion. For example, when an elephant dies the others may stroke and rearrange the bones, although why they do it is still a mystery.

Elephants are very intelligent creatures. We’ve dedicated a whole chapter to this in our new book as the findings are so important. For example, when we looked at the elephant’s brain we found that its weight was quite high compared with that of its body, which is significant.

Early on in the research we discovered that bull elephants, i.e. males, go through periods of significant change, which is called musth. This serves to advertise the male’s virility to other females, letting them know he’s healthy and would be a good father, but it also warns other males to stay away. One of the most obvious changes is in how they walk, though there are others.

However, one of our most important discoveries is that it is crucial for elephants to live for a long time. If you are a male you probably won’t be a successful mate unless you do. If you are a female, the older and more experienced you are the more likely it is that you’ll be aware of danger when it approaches. For example, an elephant may be able to cope with one lion, but may have problems if there are three of them. Age helps elephants know when it’s best to walk away or to stand and fight.

There’s a huge amount that’s still waiting to be discovered. For example, we know very little about the part that’s played in the life of elephants by their sense of smell, although we suspect that it must be important because this sense is very well developed. It’s very hard to conduct research in this area in the wild because there are so many variables involved.

Another area we know little about is illustrated by a time I observed a young elephant reaching out towards an electric fence. His mother’s whole body posture displayed alarm at the danger he was in. This is an example of how one elephant can be sensitive towards the feelings or situation of another, but we don’t know how much it happens.

analyses.content: 研究人员拥有2500头大象的数据库，知道它们的出生年月以及每一头的**母亲（mother）**是谁。
Speaker: ...we know the month and year of their birth as well as who was the mother of each one.
听到 "date of birth"（对应原文 month and year of their birth）后，紧接着就是 "who was the mother"。
Speaker: ...one thing we found from our research is that this social system is made up of a large number of different layers...
"Made up of a large number of different..." 对应题目中的 "has many..."。
研究发现大象的社会系统非常复杂，由许多不同的**层级（layers）**组成。
Speaker: We conducted an experiment in which two of the elephants brought food within reach by pulling simultaneously on the ends of a rope.
"Using a..." 对应原文的 "pulling... on the ends of a..."。
在一项实验中，两头大象通过同时拉动一根**绳子（rope）**的末端，合作获取了食物。
Speaker: A good example of this was two years ago when there was not enough rain.
"Lack of..." 对应原文的 "not enough..."。
由于缺乏雨水（rain）（即两年没下够雨），一些大象为了生存搬到了新区域。
Speaker: For example, when an elephant dies the others may stroke and rearrange the bones...
题目中的 "move" 对应原文的 "rearrange"。
当一头大象死后，其他大象可能会抚摸并重新排列它的骨头（bones）。
大象大脑的**重量（weight）**与身体相比是相当高的，这显示了它们的智慧。
Speaker: For example, when we looked at the elephant’s brain we found that its weight was quite high compared with that of its body...
"Quite high" 在原文和题目中都出现了，直接定位前面的名词 weight。
Speaker: One of the most obvious changes is in how they walk, though there are others.
"The way they..." 对应原文的 "how they..."。
公象在狂暴期（musth）最明显的变化之一是它们**走路（walk）**的方式。
Speaker: If you are a female, the older and more experienced you are the more likely it is that you’ll be aware of danger when it approaches.
"Recognize" 对应原文的 "be aware of"。
年长的雌性大象更有可能意识到**危险（danger）**的临近。
Speaker: It’s very hard to conduct research in this area in the wild because there are so many variables involved.
"Difficult to study" 对应原文的 "very hard to conduct research"。
很难在**野外（wild）**进行关于大象嗅觉的研究，因为涉及的变量太多。
Speaker: This is an example of how one elephant can be sensitive towards the feelings or situation of another...
题目结构 "How [adj] elephants are to one another" 对应原文 "how one elephant can be [adj] towards... another"。
小象接触电网的例子展示了一头大象对另一头的感受或处境是多么敏感（sensitive）。
